title: Pip's Hidden Nest
markdown:
The sky was a soft sleepy purple, dusted with the first shy stars. A breeze smelling of warm earth and clover whispered through the meadow. Pip, a tiny robin whose heart felt like a fluttering leaf, watched as Leah the builder — hands gentle as moss — and Milo the mole, who loved to tunnel and tumble, searched with him. Pip’s nest, a cradle of twigs lined with fluff, had vanished.

Leah’s voice stayed as calm as a pond. “We’ve looked behind the willow, under the mossy oak, and by the murmuring stream. Nowhere.”

Milo’s whiskers twitched. A bit of earth muffled him. “A nest can’t flutter away. Perhaps it burrowed, like I sometimes do?”

Pip chirped a small sad sound, a dewdrop falling. He missed the familiar twigs and the warm cup of the lining. He tucked his beak under his wing.

They wandered toward wild raspberry bushes, leaves mixed green and brown, the sort of tangle that made a builder’s eyes useful. Leah paused, gaze sweeping stem and shadow. “See how the leaves and twigs blend? Green hides among green stems. Brown looks like fallen sticks. If you don’t look closely, you miss the pale buds waiting for spring.” Pip hopped after them, too polite to say he had already looked everywhere a robin thought to look.

Milo put his nose to a dried leaf beside a tiny brown stem. A perfect match. “As if the leaf is trying to hide too.” He nudged a clump of dry grass; the straw-like strands tickled. “Same colour as those pebbles by the path.”

A spark arrived in Leah’s eyes, firefly-quiet. “Perhaps it isn’t missing. Hidden. Built to disappear.” She remembered a butterfly patterned like bark, almost missed on a trunk.

Milo’s mole-brain whirred, a happy beetle on a new path. “So we look for something that matches? Tree, leaves, earth?”

“Places where twigs and moss melt into bark. A nest that wants to be unseen.”

They moved slower. Eyes and noses in the same job. Milo tested the oak again and found only his own old tunnels. He tried the stream bank; wet earth, no down. Then, near an old willow, he caught the faintest hint of warm bird-fluff, the smell a nest keeps even when it pretends to be bark. Leah, now hunting shades instead of empty air, saw a cluster of moss and lichen the colour of a robin’s lining. The bark’s roughness looked like woven twigs if you let it. She did not point until she was sure, because a wrong hope would be worse than another circuit of the meadow.

“There.” Nestled against the trunk, almost a shadow that had decided to stay: browns, greys, greens, a cup among dappled light.

Pip chirped like a small bell and fluttered over. He settled with a wiggle, nudging the familiar down. Safe. Warm.

“Camouflage,” Leah said, wonder without a lecture. “Colours and patterns that belong to the tree.” She did not mention a teddy on a wooden floor.

Milo pushed a clod aside. He thought of moths that look like bark, and of himself disappearing into dark earth, and left the list unfinished. The sun dipped. Long shadows. Pip snuggled down. Leah and Milo sat until the first stars were definite, then left the willow to its trick. The meadow did not invite anyone to dream on cue. It simply went on being quiet, which was enough for a nest that had been there the whole time.
